transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
The Justice Department has dropped a lawsuit in California that sought to set aside thousands of ballots.
NPR's Jew Jothy Block reports the move comes after a series of legal losses for the federal government in the case.
The Justice Department had wanted election officials to set aside the ballots of thousands of people federal officials said were likely non-citizens but had not offered evidence.
Federal courts up to the U.S. Supreme Court rejected the Justice Department's requests before election day.
The parties were expected back in court next week, but the Justice Department wrote late Friday it's voluntarily dropping the case,
and noted by the time of the court hearing the ballots in question would already be co-mingled with other ballots.
An analysis by UCLA data experts found the federal government's list of suspected non-citizens has extensive errors,
and included names of people who are not registered to vote and others who are eligible voters.
Jew Jothy Block, NPR News.
Russia launched another round of missiles against the Ukrainian capital overnight.
The strikes came hours after President Philodomir Zelensky warned that Russia was preparing another large-scale infrastructure attack.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports the strikes are leading to widespread blackouts and water supply cutoffs.
Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said at least five people were injured and Kyiv's crucial northern bridge was damaged.
The first barrage of missiles came a few minutes before 11 p.m.
Residents received an all clear signal about 30 minutes later before another air alert came shortly after midnight with a fresh wave of missiles hitting the city.
Kyiv, the size of Berlin with a population of 3 million, has come under relentless assault in recent weeks as Russia begins its annual campaign against Ukraine's power grid.
While Ukraine lacks air defenses now, Russia is more easily financing its war after the Trump administration lifted sanctions on the sale of Russian diesel.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Krakowets, Ukraine.
It was a rocky week for Wall Street. Investors weighed the election results, a better-than-expected jobs report, and fresh concerns about artificial intelligence.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports.
Stocks initially rallied after the election. Once it became clear, Democrats had won decisively, putting to rest fears of a disputed outcome or a period of limbo.
But after buying stocks on Wednesday, investors turned around and dumped them the following day.
Political setbacks for data centers added to existing worries about the massive investment in artificial intelligence, the sell-off that began with tech stocks quickly spread to the wider market.
There was a partial rebound on Friday after the Labor Department reported solid job gains for October, but all the major stock indexes ended down for the week.
The Dow fell nearly one percent. The S&P 500 index dropped two and two-thirds percent, and the Nasdaq tumbled more than three percent.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
This is NPR News.
European officials say another round of bomb threats has targeted flights following a series of hoaxes that forced planes to divert this week.
An airport spokesperson says nine flights to or from Prague were affected Friday, and officials in France reported four threats against aircraft.
The defense minister in Hungary says fighter jets escorted three passenger planes through the country's airspace.
Three broadcasters also received security threats, but no suspicious items have been found.
Visitors to Zoo Atlanta can now see its newest giant pandas. The pair made their debut on Friday.
Marissa Meckie from member station WABE reports the city is home to one of just three U.S. zoos housing giant pandas.
Jessica Hogan lives just down the street from Zoo Atlanta, and she and her three kids come several times a week.
My one-year-old has been asking for the pandas for about a week now.
Male panda Ping Ping and female Fu Shuang made their first public appearance after arriving from China in late September.
Chinese ambassador to the U.S. Ciafeng says the pandas are a symbol of peace between the two nations.
Now there's one Chinese ambassador in D.C., but Atlanta alone boasts two panda envoys, who are both much weightier than me.
For now, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are getting to know each other and their new neighbors here in Atlanta.
For NPR News, I'm Marissa Meckie in Atlanta.
I'm Windsor Johnston, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Justice Department drops California lawsuit seeking to set aside thousands of ballots
Russia launches another missile barrage on Kyiv, injuring at least five and damaging a bridge
Wall Street stocks fall for the week after election results, AI worries, and jobs report
European officials report new bomb threats against flights, including nine affected in Prague
Zoo Atlanta debuts giant pandas Ping Ping and Fu Shuang from China
